units.citation: Ram J, Dagar JC, Lal K, Singh G, Toky OP, Tanwar VS, Dar SR, Chauhan MK (2011). Biodrainage to combat waterlogging, increase farm productivity and sequester carbon in canal command areas of northwest India. Current Science 100(11):1673-1680.
units.quote:
In spite of the decline near the tree line, overall grain 
yield of wheat in Puthi research plot was 2.2 t ha–1 (3.4 
times) compared to 0.6 t ha–1 in adjacent fields without 
plantation (Figure 5). Higher wheat yields in the research 
plot compared to untreated fields were due to lowering of 
the water table by tree plantation leading to percolation of 
rainwater. In untreated fields, high water table caused  
deficiency of oxygen and excess of carbon dioxide in the 
root zone of wheat, which finally reduced the yield.

relationship.outcome_raw: wheat grain yield (t per ha), research plot with tree strips vs adjacent waterlogged fields without plantation (3.4 times); attributed to the lowered water table letting rainwater percolate, relieving oxygen deficiency in the wheat root zone

context.practice_as_described: Biodrainage agroforestry model: four parallel strip plantations of clonal Eucalyptus tereticornis (Mysore gum, clone C-7) planted in December 2002 on raised ridges (0.5 m high) built along the field bunds of canal-irrigated, waterlogged farmers' fields at Puthi, Hisar, Haryana (northwest India). Strips were 66 m apart, each with two tree rows at 1 m x 1 m (300 plants per ha; 240 surviving); the strips occupied about 4% of the area and wheat was grown in the remaining 96% between them (p2). The deep-rooted, high-water-use trees act as 'bio-pumps' that transpire groundwater and lower the water table. BASELINE (comparator): adjacent canal-irrigated waterlogged fields without plantation (control observation wells 1 and 11; four untreated wheat fields).
context.note: Figure 5 'Wheat yield obtained with and without Eucalyptus plantation' (p7). Single season (wheat sown November 2007, harvested April 2008), quadrat (1 m x 1 m) sampling; no statistical test reported. Sowing in the untreated fields was delayed by one to two weeks by wetter soil (p3), part of the pathway. The plot-level figure already nets out the 11.7% decline near the tree lines (see ev_crop_yield_ram11_3). Supersedes the second-hand reading in ev_crop_yield_singhlal18_2.

units.citation: Kuyah et al. (2019). Agroforestry delivers a win-win solution for ecosystem services in sub-Saharan Africa. A meta-analysis. Agronomy for Sustainable Development.
units.quote: Studies on water regulation were conducted in 12 countries. In total, 96 observations were identified from 38 studies that ful- filled the selection criteria. Out of the 38 studies, 11 had 34 observations reporting on infiltration rates, while 27 studies with 62 observations reported on soil moisture content (Fig. 2). Agroforestry improved infiltration and soil moisture content compared to the control (Fig. 2). However, the effect of agrofor- estry on infiltration (RR 2.7, 95% CI 2.1–.5) was greater than that on soil moisture (RR 1.6; 95% CI 1.1–1.2). Over 90% of all the observations had RR > 1 compared to 70% for soil moisture.

Certaines études pointent le fait que le rendement de plusieurs cultures établies à proximité de haies brise-vent serait accru durant les années plus sèches (Kanzler et al., 2018; Nuberg, 1998; Thevathasan et Gordon, 2004), tandis que d’autres jugent que l’effet des haies pourrait alors nuire aux cultures non irriguées (FAO, 1986). (English: The scientific literature moreover reports no clear consensus as to the effects that windbreak hedges produce during periods of drought. Some studies point out that the yield of several crops established near windbreak hedges would be increased during drier years (Kanzler et al., 2018; Nuberg, 1998; Thevathasan and Gordon, 2004), while others judge that the effect of the hedges could then harm non-irrigated crops (FAO, 1986).)

ment of 127% (3.7 Mg CO2eq ha−1 yr−1) over full/near-full sun systems,

relationship.outcome_raw: net GHG balance (carbon dioxide removals in live biomass and soil minus nitrous oxide and methane emissions, CO2eq per ha per yr): GHG removal increment of 127% (3.7 Mg CO2eq ha−1 yr−1) in moderate-shade hybrid cocoa (Hybrid shade) over full/near-full-sun hybrid cocoa (Hybrid sun)

context.practice_as_described: Hybrid (series II) cocoa under moderate shade, 13-25 shade trees per ha of >30 cm DBH (Hybrid shade, n=30 plots, mean 22 shade trees/ha), compared with hybrid cocoa under full or near-full sun (Hybrid sun, <=6 shade trees/ha, n=50, mean 0.4). Smallholder plots in Kwaebibirem and Atiwa West, mixed with fruit trees and annual food crops on some plots; management (fertiliser, pruning, weeding, hand pollination) varies within both systems and is not held constant.
context.note: BASELINE = 'Hybrid sun': hybrid (series II) cocoa with at most 6 shade trees per ha (mean 0.4), net GHG balance -2.9 +/- 1.3 (95% CI) Mg CO2eq/ha/yr (p8; negative = net removal). Practice = 'Hybrid shade': hybrid cocoa with 13-25 shade trees per ha (mean 22), net balance -6.8 +/- 1.7 Mg CO2eq/ha/yr (abstract p1; -6.7 +/- 1.6 on p10). The quoted increment, 127% (3.7 Mg CO2eq/ha/yr), is the authors' figure; the system means above differ by about 3.9, a rounding/aggregation difference. Shown in Fig. 6a (p11), caption 'Greenhouse gases (GHGs). Panels show GHG emissions aggregated to production systems (a) and per cluster within each production system (b). Stacked bars show CO2 removals (negative emissions) by carbon sink category ..., N2O emissions by nitrogen input source ..., and CH4 emissions from cocoa-pod decomposition'. 2021 plot survey of 106 farms (30 x 30 m sub-plots) in Kwaebibirem and Atiwa West, Eastern Region; systems stratified by shade-tree density then clustered by management. Shade is NOT randomised: fertiliser, cocoa density and pollination differ between and within systems, so the shade contrast is confounded. The third system (Amazonia variety under moderate shade, -4.6) differs by variety and is not used as a shade contrast. Net balance per IPCC stock-change accounting (section 2.5); soil CO2 uptake was a fixed placeholder assumed NOT influenced by shade, so the difference is live-biomass CO2 net of N2O/CH4. Tree growth rate was the most sensitive parameter (index about 0.5); linear biomass growth assumed. CH4 was moderately higher in shaded plots because more of them piled pod husks (p13) - a post-harvest practice, not shade, so no separate unit (#39).

relationship.outcome_raw: tree/shrub leaf fodder (top feed, browse) available to sheep, goats and camels in drought years from the silvopasture trees, in addition to the understorey herbage

context.practice_as_described: Silvopasture on degraded rocky rangeland at the Central Arid Zone Research Institute (CAZRI) Range Management and Soil Conservation Centre, Bhopalgarh, Jodhpur district, Rajasthan: seven multipurpose tree and shrub species (MPTS) - Acacia tortilis, Acacia senegal, Azadirachta indica (neem), Hardwickia binata, Albizia lebbek, and the shrubs Dichrostachys nutans and Colophospermum mopane - planted in pits at 10 x 4 m spacing in 1985 (each pit refilled with soil plus farmyard manure, 10 L water per irrigation in the first two years), grass in the interspaces (Cenchrus setigerus, Dichanthium annulatum, Aristida funiculata) cut at maturity; randomised block design, three replicates, trees 14 and 15 years old at measurement (p2). BASELINE (comparator): control pasture without trees ('sole grass without tree'). Drought years 1999 and 2000 (annual rainfall about 260 mm each, against a 360 mm mean, 'highly erratic and caused drought during both the years', p2); good-rainfall reference years 1995 and 1996 taken from Singh (2000). Mechanism (in the quote): the trees and shrubs are lopped for green leaf fodder in drought years, when grass is scarce; the treeless pasture has no such browse layer. Authors' conclusion (p6): 'herbage as well as top feed production is possible during drought years for sustainable livestock production'.
context.note: Table 2 'Top feed production from 14 year old trees and shrubs' (p5): dry leaf fodder 0.08-1.85 t/ha by species (A. tortilis 1.21, A. senegal 1.01, A. indica 0.87, D. nutans 1.85 t/ha), measured in 1999, a drought year, after pruning one third of the lower crown (p2, p4). The comparator is implicit (control pasture has no tree layer) - the paper never sums top feed and herbage against the control, so no magnitude is encoded. JUDGEMENT CALL for review: kept as low-confidence direction evidence so that the trade-off (less grass, plus browse) is not reported one-sidedly.

context.note: Acronyms: AF = agroforestry, here the 25-year-old walnut alley-cropping system (pea sown in the alleys between hybrid walnut tree lines); AC = agricultural control = the same crop in full sun with no trees, in the northern part of the same parcel (the baseline); EXC = rain-excluded plots (mobile rainout shelters removed 135 mm of rain, April to end of May = the imposed spring drought); CTL = rainfed plots with normal rainfall; PARinc = cumulated incident photosynthetically active radiation over the crop cycle (MJ/m2): AC received 1,112 MJ/m2, AF quadrats 19% (south of trees) to 35% (north) less; > 920 = lighter shade, < 920 = heavier shade. Result (p7, Fig. 6 grain yield): under normal rainfall trees cut pea yield by 25-77% vs AC; under drought by only 1-47%. Absolute grain yields are shown only in Fig. 6 (not in the text layer). The light x rainfall interaction on grain yield is p < .001. Buffering of the drought IMPACT, not a yield advantage over full sun (see blan22_2). One season (2018-2019), one site (Restinclieres, southern France); AF and AC not randomised (authors note this, p3) though soil texture homogeneous; quadrats 3.5 m north and south of the tree lines (32 AF, 8 AC). The relative gain within AF partly reflects how depressed AF yields were in the rainfed arm.

units.quote:
Initially while the trees were young

relationship.outcome_raw: understorey pasture under radiata pine over the rotation: complementarity while trees were young, then the pasture disappeared entirely by about 15 years; mechanism per the authors: the trees came to dominate soil moisture (and shade) so moisture became limiting to the pasture

context.practice_as_described: radiata pine planted July 1990 in rows at 7 x 1.4 m (1,000 stems/ha), thinned to 400 stems/ha by 1994 and pruned to leave a 4 m live crown, over lucerne or ryegrass/clover (red clover dominant) pasture (forage-harvested for 3 years, then sheep-grazed), with a trees-only bare-ground treatment; compared with adjacent open-grown lucerne and ryegrass/clover pastures, all non-irrigated
context.note: Lincoln silvopasture experiment, Canterbury Plains (660 mm rain, about 60% of potential ET; summer drought common). Silvopasture and open pasture are two ADJACENT experiments analysed in separate ANOVAs, so silvopasture-vs-open contrasts are not formally tested (quasi-experimental). Neutron-probe soil moisture to 2 m, 1991-1996, growing seasons 2 to 6 after planting. 2006 site observation, not a measured yield series; open pasture is the implicit comparison. Early complementarity (land equivalent ratios above 1 in year 3) is reported second-hand from Yunusa et al. 1995a on the same experiment and is not extracted here. Authors cite similar loss in other radiata pine experiments (Knowles 1991; Hawke 1991).
